query: Which IRR statistic (Cohen’s κ, Krippendorff’s α, ICC) is best for each annotation tier and what target thresholds and adjudication rules should we set?

response.query: Which IRR statistic (Cohen’s κ, Krippendorff’s α, ICC) is best for each annotation tier and what target thresholds and adjudication rules should we set?
response.answer: Cohen’s Kappa is best for binary categorical data; Krippendorff’s α for multi-category; ICC for continuous data. Set thresholds at 0.6 for Cohen’s Kappa, 0.7 for Krippendorff’s α.

results.title: Krippendorff’s Alpha for Annotation Agreement | Label Studio
results.content: # How to Use Krippendorff’s Alpha to Measure Annotation Agreement. As a part of our inter-annotator agreement series, we’re digging into one of the most flexible and widely applicable metrics out there: Krippendorff’s alpha. Compared to other agreement metrics like Cohen’s kappa or Fleiss’ kappa, Krippendorff’s alpha offers more flexibility—and is better suited for real-world data annotation workflows. This makes it particularly useful for messy, real-world datasets where not all annotators rate every item or where the labels span beyond simple yes/no categories. Krippendorff’s alpha requires you to define an agreement metric between rating categories. Observed agreement is the average agreement across all rated items, normalized by the number of raters and label options. We’ll replace rik with the value in the table for each item i and rating k, and sum these results. Even if you don’t compute it manually, understanding how Krippendorff’s alpha works helps you choose the right agreement metric—and take action when results are low.

results.title: Annotation for computational argumentation analysis: Issues and perspectives - Lindahl - 2024 - Language and Linguistics Compass - Wiley Online Library
results.content: For all intents and purposes, argumentation mining is currently exclusively based on machine learning, that is, on methods which rely on annotated text as training data,4 in the form of large and good quality corpora. The process of marking up argumentation (or other information) in a text is in NLP called *annotation*. Hence, although many corpora follow broadly similar approaches, they vary in the details, how they model argumentation and how they evaluate their annotation. The corpora are divided as follows: In Section 3.1 corpora annotated for *argumentative text detection and stance classification* are described. This is followed by corpora annotated with models based on two of the most fundamental argumentation components: *claims* (sometimes *conclusions*) and *premises* in Section 3.2. Finally, annotation based on other types of argumentation models such as Toulmin are discussed in Section 3.4. This is discussed by Habernal and Gurevych (2017), who annotate argumentative text as a first step. Argumentative text detection and stance classification: IAA and machine-learning results (C*κ* = Cohen's *κ*, F*κ* = Fleiss's *κ*, K*α* = Krippendorff's *α*). Annotating argumentation components is a fundamental task in argumentation annotation, and using some version of a model based on claims and premises for this is probably most common. They use two corpora, Araucaria (Reed & Rowe, 2004), in which the argumentation has been annotated based on Walton's argumentation schemes (Walton et al., 2008), and a corpus of judgements from the European Court of Human Rights (Mochales & Moens, 2008). One of the most well-known argumentation corpora annotated with a claim-premise model is the persuasive essay corpus, presented by Stab and Gurevych (2017). Work using other argumentation models: IAA and machine-learning results (C*κ* = Cohen's *κ*, F*κ* = Fleiss's *κ*, K*α* = Krippendorff's *α*). There have also been experiments with machine translation of a corpus annotated for argumentation into another language, with promising results (Abbott et al., 2016; Aker & Zhang, 2017; Toledo-Ronen et al., 2020). It could also perhaps be beneficial to the field to seek inspiration from work on argumentation in linguistic discourse and conversation analysis (e.g. Paulus et al., 2018), which might bring fresh insight to the problem of argumentation annotation and mining. Revisiting computational models of argument schemes: Classification, annotation, comparison.

results.title: Introducing Krippendorff’s Alpha IAA Calculation | Datasaur
results.content: We are thrilled to announce the release of a new supported algorithm for calculating Inter-Annotator Agreement (IAA): Krippendorff's Alpha. While we have previously supported IAA calculations using Cohen's Kappa, the addition of Krippendorff's Alpha offers a robust alternative, widening the scope of applications for our users. In this blog post, we will explore the unique features of Krippendorff's Alpha and illustrate the conditions under which it excels, compared to Cohen's Kappa. Before delving into the specifics of Krippendorff's Alpha, it's important to understand the concept of Inter-Annotator Agreement. However, it has limitations when applied to tasks with more than two annotator categories or when dealing with ordinal data. Unlike Cohen's Kappa, Krippendorff's Alpha can handle multiple annotator categories, making it ideal for complex annotation tasks. This makes Krippendorff's Alpha particularly valuable in situations where there are more than two annotator categories or when dealing with ordinal data. * Multiple Categories: When the annotation task involves more than two categories, Krippendorff's Alpha provides a more accurate reflection of agreement.
